The cursor hovered over the scatter plot for eleven seconds. Then Dr. Okafor clicked. Two dots dissolved into the white void of the figure. She exhaled, saved the file as *Fig4_final_v3.pdf*, and leaned back in her chair. The lab was dark except for the blue glow of the monitor and the sodium strip above the fume hood.

Tomorrow at midnight: the NSFC submission portal locked. Three years of work. Her career's hinge.

She was pulling on her coat when the door opened.

Dr. Yoon stood in the doorway, still in her lab coat, a paper cup of cold coffee in each hand. She set one on Okafor's desk without a word. Then she pulled up the shared drive on her phone and opened the figure.

They both looked at the screen. Both looked at the two missing points—visible in the raw data spreadsheet, absent from the graph.

Yoon set the coffee down. "Is this all of the data we collected?"

The question didn't arrive loud. It arrived the way a crack arrives in ice: quiet, total, already spreading.

Okafor closed her eyes. Opened them. "Marcus—" she started, then corrected, "Yoon. Those two replicates were run on the old calibration. The spectrometer drifted in the third hour. I flagged them in the notebook. I was going to put them in the supplemental, footnote them, explain the instrument error—"

"You deleted them from the figure."

"They're *in* the file. The spreadsheet. You can open it, you'll see the raw values. I just didn't put them in the main panel because they're, they're *corrupted*, and putting corrupted data in a figure that a reviewer will screenshot and send to a colleague in Beijing who will write *instrument failure, results untrustworthy*—" Her voice cracked on the last word, thin and reedy. She pressed her palm flat on the desk. "Do you know what that does? You know what that does to the rest of it. All six years of the longitudinal cohort. Gone. Rejected in the first read. And then what? We start the protocol over. I'm fifty-one, Yoon. I don't have another six years."

Silence. The fume hood hummed.

Yoon picked up her coffee. Drank from it. It was cold. She drank from it anyway.

"Put them back," Yoon said.

Okafor stared at her. "And then we lose—"

"Put them back. And we footnote the calibration. And if the reviewer has a problem, we *answer* the problem. We don't get to decide in a dark lab at two in the morning that our data is too inconvenient for our own story." She set the cup down. "Open the figure."

Okafor's hand hovered over the mouse. The cursor blinked on the white void where two points had been.

She clicked.

They came back. Small, stubborn, true.

# Two Points

The cursor hovered over the scatter plot for eleven seconds. Then Dr. Okafor clicked. Two dots dissolved into the white void of the figure. She exhaled, saved the file as *Fig4_final_v3.pdf*, and leaned back in her chair. The lab was dark except for the blue glow of the monitor and the sodium strip above the fume hood.

Tomorrow at midnight: the NSFC submission portal locked. Three years of work. Her career's hinge.

She was pulling on her coat when the door opened.

Dr. Yoon stood in the doorway, still in her lab coat, a paper cup of cold coffee in each hand. She set one on Okafor's desk without a word. Then she pulled up the shared drive on her phone and opened the figure.

They both looked at the screen. Both looked at the two missing points—visible in the raw data spreadsheet, absent from the graph.

Yoon set the coffee down. "Is this all of the data we collected?"

The question didn't arrive loud. It arrived the way a crack arrives in ice: quiet, total, already spreading.

Okafor closed her eyes. Opened them. "Marcus—" she started, then corrected, "Yoon. Those two replicates were run on the old calibration. The spectrometer drifted in the third hour. I flagged them in the notebook. I was going to put them in the supplemental, footnote them, explain the instrument error—"

"You deleted them from the figure."

"They're *in* the file. The spreadsheet. You can open it, you'll see the raw values. I just didn't put them in the main panel because they're, they're *corrupted*, and putting corrupted data in a figure that a reviewer will screenshot and send to a colleague in Beijing who will write *instrument failure, results untrustworthy*—" Her voice cracked on the last word, thin and reedy. She pressed her palm flat on the desk. "Do you know what that does? You know what that does to the rest of it. All six years of the longitudinal cohort. Gone. Rejected in the first read. And then what? We start the protocol over. I'm fifty-one, Yoon. I don't have another six years."

Silence. The fume hood hummed.

Yoon picked up her coffee. Drank from it. It was cold. She drank from it anyway.

"Put them back," Yoon said.

Okafor stared at her. "And then we lose—"

"Put them back. And we footnote the calibration. And if the reviewer has a problem, we *answer* the problem. We don't get to decide in a dark lab at two in the morning that our data is too inconvenient for our own story." She set the cup down. "Open the figure."

Okafor's hand hovered over the mouse. The cursor blinked on the white void where two points had been.

She clicked.

They came back. Small, stubborn, true.

The fluorescent tube above Okafor's desk flickered in a rhythm she'd been tracking for forty minutes, as though the ceiling had a pulse and she was a patient. On her screen, Figure 4 glowed back at her: seven data points tracing a clean, satisfying arc. The grant—NIH R01, eleven pages, due at 11:59 p.m.—would make it through review if that arc held. If that arc held, the funding held, and the lab survived another cycle of deferred maintenance and a leaking window in Room 304.

She'd been in the data folder at 2 a.m., pulling individual .csv files into R, when she'd seen them. Two points. Point 9 and Point 14. Both from the March trial, both from subjects with the baseline comorbidity they'd never expected to see so often. Point 9 sat where the curve should have flattened. Point 14 sat below the x-axis entirely. In the raw file, they were just numbers. In the figure, they were a small catastrophe. A reviewer would ask about them. A reviewer asking about them would ask about the sample. A reviewer asking about the sample would—

She'd excluded them. Added a footnote to the methods: *n = 19, participants with comorbid conditions excluded per protocol.* The protocol did not say this. The protocol said *n = 21*. But no one would check the protocol against the raw files. No one would.

At 4:47, a shadow fell across her keyboard.

"Okafor."

Dr. Lena Vasquez stood in the doorway with two paper cups of bad vending-machine coffee, still in her lab coat, still wearing the red smudge of bromo-chloroacetic acid on her left sleeve. She set one cup on the desk without asking. Then she looked at Figure 4. She looked at the methods footnote. She looked at the .csv files still open in a tab behind the figure, where all twenty-one rows were visible, numbered, waiting.

"Is this all of the data we collected?"

The question wasn't loud. It didn't need to be. It landed in the fluorescent hum and just stayed there, vibrating.

Okafor set down her mouse. Her hands were steady, which surprised her.

"No," she said. "It isn't. I dropped the two March comorbid samples. I told myself the protocol covered it, and then I told myself you wouldn't notice, and then I told myself that if the funding doesn't come through, we can't run the next year at all, and the next year is when the actual treatment arm starts." She pulled the coffee toward her and took a sip. It was warm and tasted like burnt pennies. "I know what I did. I'm not going to pretend it's fine." She looked up at Vasquez. "Put them back. I'll rewrite the discussion. If the arc flattens, we describe a flattening. I'll explain the comorbidity. I'll take the phone call in the morning." A small, exhausted laugh. "I'd rather take the phone call than be the person who buried fourteen."

- The co-author's question is direct, confrontational

Let me think about the answer. It shouldn't be a clean "I did it, I'm sorry." That's too easy. Maybe she deflects, then the truth leaks out. Or maybe she tries to rationalize it in language that sounds scientific but is actually cover. Or maybe she's honest but defensive. Let me go with something that shows her trying to frame it as a judgment call, then the question cuts through that framing, and she stumbles into partial truth.

Let me draft this:

Setting: Late night, office, blue light of monitors. She's been working for hours. The co-author (let me name him - maybe "Marcus" or "Elliot" - let me go with "Elliot") walks in.

The two data points: maybe they show the effect wasn't as strong as the other points, or they show a slight dip that contradicts the clean trendline. For a grant application, you want the preliminary data to look promising. Two points that show the effect plateaus or dips would undermine the "clear trend" narrative.

Her answer: She should answer in a way that's evasive at first, then more honest. Something like: "I flagged them as... I excluded them because they looked like artifacts. Outliers from a bad run." But then maybe she corrects herself, or her voice drops, and she admits it was more deliberate. Or she doubles down but with a crack.

Let me aim for about 400 words. Let me write it.

Let me count carefully and make it feel real, specific, grounded.
</think>

The office smelled like cold coffee and the particular ozone hum of a monitor that had been on since four in the morning. Dr. Amara Okafor stared at Figure 4b on the grant draft—seven clean data points arcing upward, beautiful, *sufficient*—and tried to convince her own reflection in the darkened window that she'd only been tired.

The door swung open without a knock. Elliot stood in the frame, still in his running jacket, hair damp with November rain. He'd come back from the track. He always came back from the track.

He walked to the desk. Read the figure. His jaw did something small and tight.

"Is this all of the data we collected?"

Amara heard the question land flat, the way it lands when someone has already checked the folder and knows the answer before you do. He'd opened the raw data directory. She could tell. There was a particular stillness to him, a coiled quiet that meant *I'm not angry yet, but I'm not not-angry.*

She set her pen down. Picked it up. Set it down.

"Two points from the March cohort," she said. Her voice came out too steady, rehearsed, like she'd been building this sentence for the six hours she'd been staring at that graph. "They sat at 1.4 and 1.2 on the y-axis. I flagged them in the lab notebook as probable artifacts—contaminated well, degraded reagent, that kind of thing." She tapped the notebook, the real one, the one where she *had* written *degraded reagent* next to those entries in February, back when she was allowed to be uncertain. "For a preliminary figure in a grant, I thought it was reasonable to show the n=7 set. The trend is the same either way. You can put the full n=9 in the methods once we're in review."

Elliot looked at the notebook. Looked at the figure. Looked at her.

"The March cohort used the same reagent batch as the April cohort, Amara. The April points are on the graph."

The words sat between them like a small, cold animal. She opened her mouth. Closed it. The pen made a quiet click against the desk.

"Then I excluded them for reasons that are... more practical than scientific," she said, and the words tasted like ash, like swallowing a stone slowly. "The grant committee reads Figure 4b in eleven seconds, Elliot. If it plateaus, they stop reading. I can't—I can't lose this. The lab. The postdoc positions. You."

She stopped. Breathed. The monitor hummed.

"I didn't do it to hide a result. I did it to protect a *story* that's basically true. The effect is real. The trend is real. Two points in the middle of a curve that goes down slightly instead of flat." She pressed her palms flat on the desk. "But you're right. It's not all the data. And 'practical' is not a word I get to use in a methods section."

Elliot exhaled. He pulled a chair out. Sat down.

"Okay," he said. "Add them back. And we change the title of the figure."

"Change it to what?"

"To the truth. However ugly."

Amara reached for the file. The cursor blinked at the edge of the graph, patient, waiting. She clicked. The two points appeared in the upper left, small and stubborn, pulling the line into a shape that was less a rocket and more a hill. A real hill. One you had to actually climb.

She saved the file. The window showed her face, older than it had an hour ago, and she looked at it for a long time before turning back to the screen.

# Two Points

The lab was quiet except for the hum of the fume hood and the particular silence that fills a room after 11 p.m., when the rest of the building has gone to sleep. Dr. Amara Okafor sat at her desk, staring at the revised Figure 4 on her monitor. Two points gone. Two little dots that had been sitting at the far right of the scatter plot, stubbornly off the regression line, stubbornly *wrong* for the story the grant narrative needed.

She'd removed them at 10:47 p.m. with a small, clinical selection in Python. No comment in the code. No note to self. Just *df.drop(index=[14, 19])* and a save.

The door clicked open. Marcus Yuen appeared in the frame, coffee cup in hand, reading glasses pushed up into his curly hair. He'd been in the building all night too, it seemed. He'd seen her lights on.

He set the coffee on her desk and pulled up the shared file on her second monitor. Scrolled to Figure 4. Tilted his head.

Then he looked at her.

"Is this all of the data we collected?"

The question wasn't accusatory. It was flat, factual, the tone a person uses when reading a lab notebook and noticing a gap in the sequence of entries. But it landed like a hand on the back of her neck.

Amara's throat went dry. She could say *yes* and the word would come out clean, because she had, in fact, been very precise about the language. She hadn't *hidden* anything. She'd *curated*. The two points were from a batch where the spectrometer calibration had drifted; she could explain that. She *would* explain that, if anyone asked follow-up questions, which they wouldn't, because the grant reviewers would never look that closely at the raw data, and the figure was clean, and the R-squared was beautiful, and the deadline was in fourteen hours and she had not slept in thirty-one.

She opened her mouth. Closed it.

Marcus was still watching her. Not smirking. Not angry. Just waiting, the way he waited when a reaction was supposed to complete at a certain time and the color change hadn't happened yet. Patient. Slightly worried.

Amara exhaled.

"Two of them aren't in there," she said. Her voice came out lower than she intended. "Points fourteen and nineteen from the March run. The calibration on the 780 had drifted by about two nanometers after the ninth sample, and I didn't re-zero it. So those two readings are technically artifacts. I pulled them."

A pause. Marcus set his coffee down. Picked it up again. Set it down.

"And you didn't flag them in the methods?"

"I was going to. In the next pass."

"The next pass is the grant, Amara. The grant is *tomorrow.*"

"I know."

He nodded slowly. Didn't reach for his laptop. Didn't open the raw files to confirm. He just nodded, the way you nod when you're deciding whether a crack in the foundation is structural or cosmetic, and you don't have a flashlight yet.

"Put them back," he said. Not a question.

Amara looked at the figure. The regression line was so clean. So *good.*

She opened the notebook.

It was 11:34 p.m. She had thirteen hours left, and the line was going to be ugly, and she was going to have to rewrite the abstract, and the reviewers were going to see the wobble and maybe, *maybe*, still say yes.

She typed the index numbers back in.

# Figure 4

The cursor blinked at 2:17 a.m. on a Tuesday, and Dr. Adaeze Okafor deleted the last two markers from the scatter plot. She didn't export. Didn't save. Just deleted them in the open file, and the R² climbed from 0.61 to 0.83, and the trend line straightened into something that looked, for the first time, like the clean arc her proposal described.

She told herself it was a modeling choice. The two points came from the batch where the reagent had degraded, and she *could* have logged them as QC failures. She *could* have. She'd had four hours of sleep and a deadline in nine hours, and the reviewer's email from March still lived in her inbox: *"Insufficient preliminary data to support the proposed mechanism."*

She saved the figure. Wrote the methods paragraph without the QC sentence. Went to bed in a t-shirt and slippers and dreamed, briefly, of her mother's kitchen in Enugu, the smell of palm oil, her father's voice saying *you don't get to skip the middle part just because the end looks prettier.*

---

At 8:45, Yuki Tanaka, her postdoc, sat across from her in the cramped office with a printed copy of the figure on the desk between them. Yuki had been looking at the raw CSV for twenty minutes. She wasn't angry. That was the worst part. She was just *looking.*

"Adaeze." A pause. "Is this all of the data we collected?"

The question was flat. No accusation in it. That made it worse.

Adaeze opened her mouth. The modeling-choice line was already shaped on her tongue, the QC-failure justification, the part where the degraded reagent made the points *technically* invalid. She could have said all of that. She had rehearsed it in the shower.

She looked at the printed figure. The clean line. The beautiful, straight little line that would get them the grant.

"No," she said.

Yuki waited.

"No," Adaeze repeated, and her voice came out smaller than she intended, scraped thin. "I dropped two. From the June batch. I told myself it was a quality flag. I told myself a lot of things." She pressed her thumb against the edge of the desk. "I'm going to put them back. I'm going to put them back and we're going to write up what the data actually says, and if the mechanism is weaker than the proposal, then we write that the mechanism is weaker than the proposal."

Yuki nodded slowly. Folded the printed page. Set it face-down on the desk.

"The deadline," she said, not quite a question.

"I know." Adaeze picked up her phone. Typed *Dear Dr. Whitfield, I will need to submit a revised preliminary dataset—* and deleted it. Typed it again.

She didn't hit send for a long time. But she hit send.

The fluorescent tube above Marcus's desk buzzed its one flat note, the only sound in the lab past eleven. Dr. Adaeze Okafor stood in the doorway, her coat still on, one heel tapping the linoleum in a rhythm that meant *I should leave, I should leave, I should leave.*

Marcus didn't look up from his monitor. He was rotating the Figure 4 panel, zooming, zooming back out. The scatter plot of cortisol responses. Clean. Beautiful. A tight upward trend that would make the NIH reviewers weep.

"You moved the x-axis," he said. Not an accusation. Just an observation, the way a man notes a crack in a windshield.

"The range is more legible at that scale."

He let that sit. Then he opened the raw CSV from the March cohort, the one sitting in the shared drive, unedited, timestamped 11:47 a.m. like every other honest file in the folder. He cross-referenced. His jaw did something small.

"Two of the March six subjects aren't in the figure," he said. "Subject 14. Subject 22. The ones with the flat-line responses."

The tapping stopped.

"Is this all of the data we collected?" he asked. He said it the way you ask if the oven is actually off after you've already turned the burner down. No performance. Just a man needing a straight answer before he could breathe.

Adaeze set her keys on the counter. The little jingle sounded obscenely cheerful. She pulled off her coat, hung it on the back of a chair, sat down at the edge of his desk with the careful slowness of someone setting down something heavy.

"No," she said. And then, because the first word was not enough: "No. And I know what it is, and I know what it isn't. They weren't *bad* data. They were *inconvenient* data. Subject 14 was on a new med. Subject 22 had a sleep debt from the prior night. I told myself I was just *contextualizing the sample.* I told myself the trend held without them. I told myself that two points out of thirty-eight wouldn't change the story."

She looked at the screen. The clean line. The beautiful lie wearing a clean line's face.

"I did it because the deadline is tomorrow, Marcus. And because I am *tired.* And because if I put those two dots in there, the slope drops, and the p-value gets iffy, and I spend the next eighteen months writing another R01 instead of *this* one, the one that was supposed to fund the lab for three years. So. No. It is not all the data. And I'm sorry. And I'm not asking you to let it slide."

The tube buzzed. Marcus closed the CSV.

"Put them back," he said. "And I'll re-run the stats. We'll talk to the reviewers about the n=2 outlier conditions. We'll survive."

Adaeze picked up her keys. The tapping resumed, but slower now. Less like a countdown. More like a pulse finding its way back to something honest.

The cursor blinked in the corner of the figure like a metronome keeping time for something she didn't want to acknowledge.

Two dots that, if left in place, would give the whole thing the look of a question rather than an answer.

She'd told herself they were artifacts. Repipetting errors. The kind of noise every lab generated and every PI waved away. She'd even written a note in the lab notebook at 1:47 AM: *concentrations 0.8/1.2 — likely pipetting inconsistency, to be verified in next batch.* She'd written it so fast her handwriting had gone sloppy, almost cursive, as if speed could make it true.

It wasn't the whole truth. The pipette had been calibrated. She knew that now, with a clarity that arrived too late and would not leave. But the sentence was out, and it held the shape of a defense, and Jonah was already nodding slowly, writing something in his notebook, and the cursor blinked on, patient, indifferent, keeping time for the three hours they still had.

The lab had that particular silence at 11:40 p.m., the kind where only the centrifuge hummed and the overhead fluorescents buzzed like a trapped insect. Dr. Amara Okafor stared at Figure 4 on her screen. The curve swept upward, clean and convincing, exactly what the NSERC panel would want to see. Exactly what would keep the lab funded for three more years.

Except it hadn't always looked like that.

Out. She'd told herself it was exploratory. She'd told herself there were *legitimate* reasons: subject 17 had been mid-antibiotic, subject 22 had a confounding autoimmune flare she'd noted in the raw log. Reasonable exclusions. Amara set her mouse down. Her hands were steady, which surprised her.

"Then let's look at 17 and 22 together," he said. "Right now. Before you talk yourself into the wrong answer again."

Amara turned the screen toward him. The centrifuge hummed. The fluorescents buzzed. Outside, the first grey light of a very early morning was beginning to bruise the windows.

# The Hold

The cursor blinked at the end of the caption she'd typed. Figure 4A. Twenty-three data points arranged in a clean ascending arc, the kind of curve that made reviewers say *compelling*. The kind that made the narrative in the grant proposal—the one she'd spent four months building, the one that justified $1.2 million in funding—hold together.

She'd removed the two points at 11:14. Just dragged them off the scatter plot into a folder she'd labeled *hold* in her Documents. Not deleted. Not destroyed. Just… not there. Point 19 and Point 20, the two replicates from the Thursday run that had flatlined, that had refused to rise with the rest of the cohort, that would sit at the bottom of the y-axis like two small accusations.

Her phone read 11:47. Submission portal closed at 8 AM.

She was reaching for her coffee—cold, three days old—when the lab door creaked.

Lena stood in the doorway, coat still on, a manila folder under one arm. She'd been at the hospital. Okafor could tell by the particular set of her shoulders, the way she hadn't yet let the day's exhaustion reach her face.

"You're still here." Not a question.

"Final pass on the figures."

Lena crossed the room, set the folder on the desk, leaned on the back of Okafor's chair. She didn't look at the screen until she was close enough to read it. Her eyes tracked the arc. She was quiet for a long time.

"That's twenty-three points."

"The assay ran twenty-five times."

Another silence. The fluorescent tube above the fume hood hummed its single flat note.

Lena straightened. Her voice didn't rise. It didn't have to. "Is this all of the data we collected?"

Okafor's hand was still wrapped around the coffee mug. The ceramic was warm through the ring stain of four hours. She opened her mouth. The first sentence she formed—*the Thursday run had a contamination issue, I can't say I'm confident in those two replicates*—died in her throat. It wasn't true. The Thursday run was clean. She'd checked the controls twice.

She set the mug down.

"No. It isn't. Points nineteen and twenty are in a folder on this machine. I pulled them an hour ago because the deadline is in eight hours and I was tired and I was scared the story would fall apart without them." She swallowed. "I was going to put them back. "Then put them back now. And rewrite the narrative. The curve bends, but it still goes up. They'll still fund you."

Okafor looked at the screen. At the folder labeled *hold*. At the two points waiting in it like a held breath.

She dragged them back onto the plot.

The arc broke. And held. And went up.
